pr_body:
> Follow-ups in https://github.com/nodejs/node/issues/49148

## Follow-up from the comments:

@cjihrig:

- [x] Using a custom path instead of .env file in the current working directory.
- [ ] The option to augment vs. overwrite the existing process.env with the values from the .env file. If we support augmenting, what happens on conflict (overwrite, don’t overwrite, throw, etc.)?
- [ ] ~~Programmatic API~~.
- [ ] ~~The ability to put the loaded values in an object other than process.env.~~
- [ ] ~~Multiline values.~~
- [x] Comments in the .env files.
- [ ] ~~Variable expansion.~~

@KhafraDev 

- [x] regarding testing and validation, you can take dotenv’s test suite https://github.com/motdotla/dotenv/tree/master/tests

@GeoffreyBooth 

- [x] the flag should be –env-file [path-to-file] so like –env-file .env or –env-file .env.development or whatever.
- [x] fix and support windows newline character
- [x] Support `NODE_OPTIONS`

## Missing features

The following features are not implemented in this current context. And can be implemented in a separate PR.

- Respect newline character in values with `"`
- Multiline values
- Variable expansion
- Incremental env support (.env.development overrides .env on NODE_ENV=development)

Ref: https://github.com/orgs/nodejs/discussions/44975

- Using a custom path instead of `.env` file in the current working directory.

I think it’s okay if we define our scope as more limited than `dotenv`‘s, and if people want something more full-featured then they should just use `dotenv`. Ultimately the point of adding this is to fix https://github.com/nodejs/node/issues/48852 and https://github.com/nodejs/node/pull/43973, to just provide a way to configure Node, and the ability to set other environment variables beyond `NODE_OPTIONS` is a side benefit.

That said, from your [list](https://github.com/nodejs/node/pull/48890#issuecomment-1646746252) I already mentioned allowing specifying the path to the file, and I think we need to at least document what we do for conflicts; I think the simplest approach is to just always have the “real” environment variable win out over whatever is defined in the file, and leave it at that. What is this feature's interaction with the permission model?

> What is this feature's interaction with the permission model?

@panva If we want to support NODE_OPTIONS, it needs to bypass permission model, since V8 will not be initialized at that time.

> @panva If we want to support NODE_OPTIONS, it needs to bypass permission model, since V8 will not be initialized at that time.

So an `env` variable that pretty much can override node options... That is honestly risky in many fronts even more when it boils down to bypassing permission mode options.
@nodejs/tsc This seems like the kind of thing the TSC should have an opinion on.

> > @panva If we want to support NODE_OPTIONS, it needs to bypass permission model, since V8 will not be initialized at that time.
> 
> So an `env` variable that pretty much can override node options… That is honestly risky in many fronts even more when it boils down to bypassing permission mode options.

1. If `NODE_OPTIONS` is set as an environment variable, it will take precedence over whatever’s loaded from a file. So if that’s the way that permissions are being enabled, it still will be.

2. If permissions are being enabled via flag only, so like running `node --experimental-permissions --env-file .env` where `.env` defines a `NODE_OPTIONS` without mentioning permissions, permissions will still get enabled. The `NODE_OPTIONS` in the file doesn’t “turn off” flags set directly. It’s additive, just like if you run `NODE_OPTIONS=--enable-source-maps node --inspect app.js` you get both source maps and debugging enabled.

3. [`--experimental-permission`](https://nodejs.org/api/cli.html#--experimental-permission) only controls access to the filesystem, child processes and worker threads; there’s no way to restrict Node’s access to environment variables, other than spawning a child process with explicitly set environment variables. Running `node --experimental-permissions --env-file .env app.js` would mean you’re starting Node without the ability to read files, since `--allow-fs-read` isn’t passed, but you’re _also_ passing `--env-file` which is explicitly telling Node to read a particular file; I don’t view this as a contradiction or a violation of the permissions model because the user is opting into it at the same place they’re enabling the permissions model.

All that said, we should have tests for all of the above.

For context, we've discussed support for environment variables at https://github.com/nodejs/security-wg/issues/993.

Regardless if you are passing `--env-file`, I believe you should explicitly allow access to the environment file (through --allow-fs-read). For instance, see this happening with `--experimental-policy`:

```console
$ node --experimental-permission --allow-fs-read=/home/rafaelgss/repos/os/node/t.js --experimental-policy=policy.json t.js

```

Reading the referenced discussion - https://github.com/orgs/nodejs/discussions/44975, I thought that the main motivation for adding this functionality to Node.js is to enable users to configure Node.js using a file by overriding the `NODE_OPTIONS` env var. Since `NODE_OPTIONS` support has been removed, I'm not sure I understand what problem this PR is solving because we can do the same thing using the dotenv Npm package. If there's any other motivation for this change, could you please add that to the PR description?

Also, if we really need to have a way to configure Node.js using a file, did we consider having an actual config file that just configures the Node.js runtime instead of focusing on modifying the environment variables of the application code? I think that would at least have a nicer UI because if we use the `.env` file approach that is proposed in this PR, once we have `NODE_OPTIONS` support, the way to configure Node.js would be add a line like this:

```
NODE_OPTIONS="--max-http-header-size=102400 --force-node-api-uncaught-exceptions-policy"
```

So it has potential of turning into a really big line which I think can be improved if we change the format of the config file into something like this:

```json
{
  "experimentalPolicy": true,
  "maxHttpHeaderSize": 102400,
  "forceNodeApiUncaughtExceptionsPolicy": true
}
```

@RaisinTen, my understanding is that `NODE_OPTIONS` support is there, but not "destructured" in the way you're talking about (i.e., the env variable within `.env` is still `NODE_OPTIONS`, which a string value) afaik the main difference here is that CLI options have higher precedence over the `NODE_OPTIONS` env value and `NODE_OPTIONS` `.env` value.

I do like the destructuring of `NODE_OPTIONS` into individual `.env` properties, but:

* `.env` is not in a JSON format but rather the usual "ini/cfg" format we see for plain text files.
* Doing such destructuring has its side effects, i.e. conflict with userland environment variables with the same name (Even tho I do not think environment variables would ever be in camel-case or at least that doesn't sound like a common approach)

> I thought that the main motivation for adding this functionality to Node.js is to enable users to configure Node.js using a file 

It is. We've been discussing this PR privately and for now the plan is to land this when it's ready but tag it as "don't release," and add `NODE_OPTIONS` support in a follow up. Once that lands we'll release both.

Supporting easier to read config file formats like JSON can come later. This approach was chosen because it seemed likely to succeed in that it felt realistic to be able to implement in C++ at the point when we would need to parse the file in time to be able to configure Node, before V8 has started.

Do we agree that having a dedicated file for configuring the Node.js runtime using an easier to read config file format like JSON would be more preferred than putting the options in a `NODE_OPTIONS` string in the `.env` file proposed here? I'm trying to understand if supporting that is the ultimate end goal or if we plan to land this, add `NODE_OPTIONS` support, release this and in addition to supporting the `.env` file, optionally start supporting a JSON config file for the Node.js runtime options later on.

> Supporting easier to read config file formats like JSON can come later. This approach was chosen because it seemed likely to succeed in that it felt realistic to be able to implement in C++ at the point when we would need to parse the file in time to be able to configure Node, before V8 has started.

When you say "before V8 has started", are you referring to the time before the Isolate used for running the application code gets created? If so, we can make use of https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/main/src/json_parser.h in C++ to parse the JSON. Internally, it makes use of a temporary short-lived Isolate instance which doesn't get used for running application code. So this too sounds equally realistic to implement, right?

Would `NODE_OPTIONS` still be restricted to a subset of options, or would it allow any options when loaded from `.env`? I assume it's the former because the latter would add yet more complexity.

> Do we agree that having a dedicated file for configuring the Node.js runtime using an easier to read config file format like JSON would be more preferred than putting the options in a `NODE_OPTIONS` string in the `.env` file proposed here?

I am not sure what problem this is solving. Ideally, users should not have to use `NODE_OPTIONS`. I assume that most manual invocations of `node` don't, and most other invocations (in non-trivial development environments and in production environments) can either use the environment variable or just pass the options as CLI arguments as part of an npm script or so.

> Do we agree that having a dedicated file for configuring the Node.js runtime using an easier to read config file format like JSON would be more preferred than putting the options in a `NODE_OPTIONS` string in the `.env` file proposed here?

Why not both? Being able to load environment variables from a file is its own use case and benefit. What Node can do in core that `dotenv` can’t do is support `NODE_OPTIONS` set from such a file, hence this PR.

Providing the ability to configure Node via something more ergonomic than a `NODE_OPTIONS` line in a file would be preferable, yes, but not a reason to not support both approaches IMO. It’s not like if we add support for configure-via-JSON then we would deprecate `NODE_OPTIONS`.

The reason that the `.env` file approach was chosen for this initial effort was:
- There wouldn’t need to be any design effort involved in debating the ideal JSON (or other file type) schema. `NODE_OPTIONS` is already defined.
- The goal is to support all the Node options that `NODE_OPTIONS` currently supports, and many of those configure V8, so this parsing needs to happen quite early in the Node startup process, before V8 is initialized. Others mentioned that we use V8 to parse JSON, hence the idea to use the `.env` file format as parsing it via C++ code could be done with reasonably low effort and without needing V8 or bulky libraries. If it’s possible to parse JSON at the same point in startup without needing V8 and without needing to write mountains of code, great; that just means it would be easy to add JSON config file support in addition in the future.

Or to put it another way, say that there was an open PR that adds support for configuring Node via JSON, and there was unanimous agreement that the proposed JSON schema was perfect. Say that that PR landed and was released. Would you be opposed to a following PR that added support for loading environment variables from a file, including configuring Node via `NODE_OPTIONS` in such a file? I think such an addition would be welcome; the two features complement each other, in my opinion, so we should release whichever one is ready first.

> if we plan to land this, add `NODE_OPTIONS` support, release this and in addition to supporting the `.env` file, optionally start supporting a JSON config file for the Node.js runtime options later on.

Yes, that is what I have in mind.

> Would `NODE_OPTIONS` still be restricted to a subset of options

The goal would be to support any options that `NODE_OPTIONS` supports. There is a surprisingly long list of flags that `NODE_OPTIONS` lacks support for, such as `--import`, but adding support for those should be its own effort (and affect both `NODE_OPTIONS` as loaded from an environment variable or as loaded from an `.env` file). Presumably once `--env-file` is released, there will be more interest in updating `NODE_OPTIONS` to add support for the various flags that it doesn’t currently allow.

@ovflowd 

> * Doing such destructuring has its side effects, i.e. conflict with userland environment variables with the same name (Even tho I do not think environment variables would ever be in camel-case or at least that doesn't sound like a common approach)

I wanted to clarify that what I'm suggesting only sets the camel-case versions of the Node.js runtime CLI options - https://nodejs.org/api/cli.html#options to configure only the Node.js runtime and not the rest of the application code because dotenv already allows configuring the application code and the main motivation of this change is to configure the Node.js runtime. In https://github.com/nodejs/node/pull/48890#issuecomment-1646748456 @GeoffreyBooth said:

> Ultimately the point of adding this is to fix https://github.com/nodejs/node/issues/48852 and https://github.com/nodejs/node/pull/43973, to just provide a way to configure Node, and the ability to set other environment variables beyond `NODE_OPTIONS` is a side benefit.

I don't have much context on the second issue but if you look at the first issue, the complain is about the lengthiness of this line in the `package.json` npm script and how this makes it hard to read:

```json
    "test": "c8 node --test --test-reporter @reporters/junit --test-reporter-destination=junit.xml --test-reporter spec --test-reporter-destination stdout"
```

I don't think the `.env` file approach suggested here is the right fix for this issue because if we have `NODE_OPTIONS` support in the `.env` file, the line would look like this (provided all of these options are supported in `NODE_OPTIONS`):

```txt
NODE_OPTIONS="--test --test-reporter @reporters/junit --test-reporter-destination=junit.xml --test-reporter spec --test-reporter-destination stdout"
```

which is not very different from the original npm script. This is still hard to read for the user because it is still a big line.

If we use the JSON format I suggested, the config would look like this:

```json
{
  "test": true,
  "testReporter": "@reporters/junit",
  "testReporterDestination": "junit.xml",
  "testReporter": "spec",
  "testReporterDestination": "stdout"
}
```

Since this doesn't have the huge line anymore, I think this approach would solve the problem.

@GeoffreyBooth 

> Why not both?

> Would you be opposed to a following PR that added support for loading environment variables from a file, including configuring Node via `NODE_OPTIONS` in such a file?

I'm not opposed to this. I just feel that if this turns into a complete solution for reading all env vars from a file, it's going to be more complicated than what I suggested. I didn't think that the complexity is really justified because dotenv already solves most of the problem except for the case of a single environment variable - `NODE_OPTIONS` and that isn't a blocker for folks if they want to use it because folks could still do `NODE_OPTIONS=... node file-that-uses-dotenv.js` or `node --...node options... file-that-uses-dotenv.js` either in the CLI or in an npm script. I wanted to run the alt solution I had in my mind by you because it felt like a nicer solution for the key problem and I thought that you might be willing to switch to this approach because as you said, the goal is to configure Node.js and not the other env vars because that's just a side-benefit. However, if you still want to support both, sure.

> However, if you still want to support both, sure.

I want to support something _soon._ I don’t see the config file approach landing in less than months or years, because people will debate the schema for JSON, or they’ll ask for alternate formats like JSON with comments, or god forbid they’ll want to be able to run JavaScript that returns an object—all the config file variations that popular JS tools support, that would be hard for us to implement in C++. If someone has the bandwidth to shepherd a discovery and design and implementation process to navigate all of that and get a config file approach approved and landed, great, go do it; but this version is something simple that we can ship within a matter of days.

> If we use the JSON format I suggested, the config would look like this:
> 
> ```json
> {
>   "test": true,
>   "testReporter": "@reporters/junit",
>   "testReporterDestination": "junit.xml",
>   "testReporter": "spec",
>   "testReporterDestination": "stdout"
> }
> ```
> 
> Since this doesn't have the huge line anymore, I think this approach would solve the problem.

@RaisinTen FWIW, this might solve one particular problem, but your example violates RFC 8259, which defines that names within an object SHOULD be unique (even though ECMA-404 technically allows your suggestion).

Quick note: After digging through Node.js' execution flow, I don't think it's not possible to support `--experimental-permission` in `--env-file` if we want to support `NODE_OPTIONS` flag in `.env` files. cc @RafaelGSS 

Upon reviewing all the positive feedback from people interested in this PR, I think we should add `.env` support even without NODE_OPTIONS. The implementation is simple enough to not bloat the code, but touches an important part to make people (including me) get excited.

Regarding the desire to not have everything in one line, the following shell script works on my machine:

```shell
#!/bin/bash

export NODE_OPTIONS="--disable-proto=delete \
  --frozen-intrinsics"

node --print "Object.prototype.__proto__" # Default is null, with --disable-proto=delete it’s undefined
```

When run in current Node 20, I get:

```shell
undefined
(node:47892) ExperimentalWarning: The --frozen-intrinsics flag is experimental
(Use `node --trace-warnings ...` to show where the warning was created)
```

Which I think means that Node parsed both flags. Now maybe part of how this is working is that the shell interpreter is treating the backslash-newline as an escaped character, and a “real” environment variable with newlines wouldn’t work this way. But I think our `--env-file` parser can just behave the way the shell does, and replace backslash-newline with a space or an empty string. Then people can define `NODE_OPTIONS` across multiple lines.

Anyway this is for the follow-up that adds `NODE_OPTIONS` support. I still think this PR is worth landing on its own, and if there’s some reason we can’t land the follow-up then we can debate if we want to keep this part by itself.
I would note that this should support _all_ environment variables defined in https://nodejs.org/api/cli.html#environment-variables.

The collaborator instructions contain this very short paragraph:

https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/d150316a8ecad1a9c20615ae62fcaf4f8d060dcc/onboarding.md?plain=1#L165-L172

As you say, "dotenv is at 35 million download weekly", so there is clear evidence that whatever the dotenv package is being used for can very well be done outside of Node.js core. (If this PR were to support all relevant environment variables that Node.js and its dependencies use, that might fall under the second point. But is that subset of features popular?)

There is also [a document on the project's technical values](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/main/doc/contributing/technical-values.md), which lists under developer experience:

> Bundling friction-reducing APIs and components, even though they could be provided externally

Clearly, setting environment variables could be done externally and rather trivially so, but perhaps for some folks, this PR _might_ reduce friction.

> there is clear evidence that whatever the dotenv package is being used for can very well be done outside of Node.js core

Same can be said about test framework, assertions, app watching and CLI parameter reading, and yet we are where we are, so these guidelines seem to be quite outdated by now, and perhaps would benefit from revisiting.

"All the basic functionality is already baked into the standard library and I don't need to bring 90000 dependencies to get obvious functionality in" is consistently being brought up as the reasons why people choose Deno and Bun over Node.js, hence my argument with regards to what constitutes an obvious functionality.

issue_context.title: Add test runner configuration
comments: this was raised before some people had concerns, but I am definitely +1 on this @nodejs/test_runner WDYT?

This came up recently in https://github.com/nodejs/node/pull/48425#issuecomment-1638658933. See also https://github.com/orgs/nodejs/discussions/44975 and https://github.com/nodejs/node/pull/43973 (the latter is very similar to this feature request).

I would love to see Node be configurable via `package.json` or some other config file, but I think such configuration needs to cover _all_ of Node’s configuration[^1], not just a subset like the test runner or [loaders](https://github.com/nodejs/node/pull/43973). This is tricky because a lot of Node’s configuration gets used during startup by C++ code, so any implementation needs to read and parse the config file before the first config value gets used. In the discussion elsewhere we think that the easiest way to achieve this would be to give Node [support for `.env` files](https://github.com/orgs/nodejs/discussions/44975) like Bun already has, as this would let people define Node’s config as a `NODE_OPTIONS` variable within such a file, as well as any other environment variables an app needs (as in, it solves not only the “configure Node” use case but also the “configure app” use case). It’s probably also easier to write C++ to parse a `.env` file than a JSON file. We can also always add support for configuration from `package.json` or elsewhere _in addition_ to the `.env` file, just as Bun supports multiple config files.

[^1]: Or realistically, all of Node’s configuration supported by the `NODE_OPTIONS` environment variable. There are a handful of command line flags that are unsupported there, that presumably would be unsupported by a config file as well.

I'm +0.5, but can someone make the case of what's the difference between having a config file that also calls `run` and just having a config file? Like, other than "that's what other runners do" what's the rationale?

It makes sense to me to support more options than just those for the test runner.

I am not familiar with Node internals, so if parsing JSON is hard at the level it’s needed, I’m inclined to believe whatever you tell me.

I am personally just not a fan of `.env` files though. They can only contain string key-value pairs, but sometimes another type makes more sense. For example, for to map reporters to the output files, it makes sense to use a map / object. I saw https://github.com/orgs/nodejs/discussions/44975#discussioncomment-3881320, which proposes to add more environment variables. I think this makes it better, but still, this looks weird to me:

```sh
NODE_TEST_REPORTER='@reporters/junit spec'
NODE_TEST_REPORTER_DESTINATION='junit.xml stdout'
```

---

> what's the difference between having a config file that also calls `run` and just having a config file?

One useful feature of `node --test`, is that test files can also be explicitly passed as a command line argument. Having a configuration, it could be possible to run `node path/to/specific.test.js`, and still have the configuration applied. Also `run()` currently doesn’t accept `reporters`.

Also if such a configuration is standardized, third party integrations such as editor integrations could read this configuration. If we take the configuration a bit further, it could look like this:

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "test": "c8 node --test"
  },
  "test": {
    "loaders": ["tsx"],
    "testNamePatterns": "test/*.ts"
    "reporters": {
      "@reporters/junit": "junit.xml",
      "spec": "stdout"
    }
  }
}
```

This would tell all integrations to use the `tsx` loader.

Strongly -1 for extending package.json or another kind of 'hardcoded' config. My own 'test-runner' implementation is about 100 lines for all: test.config.xxx (js, mjs or ts) parsing, setup ESM loaders, collecting coverage via c8 Report class, choosing right reporters for CI, etc. Everyone can write something similar and publish as NPM package.

Moreover, we can ask @MoLow to add his own implementation (with package.json support or whatever) following the example of 'reporters' repo, which can be used as default solution for 80% of Node users. Sometimes this configuration tool may come bundled with Node, or deprecated in favour of 'full-featured configuration system for Node' in 2030.

> Also `run()` currently doesn’t accept `reporters`.

It accepts - trough 'setup' callback: root.reporter.compose(reporter).pipe(your destination).

> Moreover, we can ask @MoLow to add his own implementation (with package.json support or whatever) following the example of 'reporters' repo, which can be used as default solution for 80% of Node users. Sometimes this configuration tool may come bundled with Node, or deprecated in favour of 'full-featured configuration system for Node' in 2030.

I am pretty sure this is something that cannot happen in userland. flags are parsed before execution of any js code

> > Moreover, we can ask @MoLow to add his own implementation (with package.json support or whatever) following the example of 'reporters' repo, which can be used as default solution for 80% of Node users. Sometimes this configuration tool may come bundled with Node, or deprecated in favour of 'full-featured configuration system for Node' in 2030.
> 
> I am pretty sure this is something that cannot happen in userland. flags are parsed before execution of any js code

You are definitely right... for regular Node usage. But 'run' is a bit different thing: each test file executed as separate process, so we can specify any options via process.env.NODE_OPTIONS = '...' then call 'run' - and it works.
